description: RF Echoes is led by an RF & antenna engineering student (Erasmus Mundus EMIMEP, future thesis at Keysight on phased arrays for LEO satellites). We tackle “Dancing with the SARs” using Sentinel-1 radar data to reveal changes on Earth’s surface. We welcome teammates with Python, data analysis, remote sensing or visualization skills. Beginners motivated by space and radar are welcome too!
summary: I am an RF and antenna engineering student, so I wanted to look at Earth the way a radar does: not with light, but with echoes. Doñana's Radar Waltz is an interactive web app that follows the seasonal "dance" of water, rice and wetlands in Doñana, southern Spain, using SAR backscatter. You can play the four seasons, swipe winter against summer, show open water and see where the surface changed. The rice fields of Isla Mayor lead the dance: dark in winter, flooded in spring, bright in summer. Seasonal open water peaks at 76 km² in spring. Doñana is a UNESCO wetland under water stress, and radar can watch it even when clouds hide it. NISAR's L-band will see further, under the vegetation.
details:
Why this project

In my master (Erasmus Mundus EMIMEP, Limoges, Brescia, Bilbao) I work on antennas and microwave systems, and my master thesis at Keysight (Feb-Aug 2027) is on calibration of phased arrays for LEO satellites. A SAR is exactly that kind of system: an antenna that sends a pulse and listens to the echo. For this challenge I wanted to go from the hardware side to what the echo tells us about the ground.

Why Doñana

I live in Spain, and Doñana is one of the most important wetlands in Europe. Its water is shared between nature, rice farming and fish ponds, and its marshes have been under strong pressure in recent years. Clouds often cover it in the wet season, which makes it a good case for radar.

What the app does

- Four seasonal radar images (Dec 2019 to Nov 2020) with a "Play the waltz" animation.

- Two views: VV backscatter in grey, and a VV/VH colour composite where green shows vegetation (volume scattering).

- A water layer: calm water reflects the pulse away from the satellite (specular reflection), so it looks dark. Pixels below -17 dB in VV are classified as open water. Water present in all four seasons is permanent (sea, river, ponds); the rest is seasonal.

- A change map (summer VV minus winter VV): red where the surface becomes brighter, blue where it becomes darker.

- A winter/summer swipe, coordinates on hover, a seasonal water chart and short explanations for non-experts.

What I found

- The strongest rhythm is human: the Isla Mayor rice fields. In summer the rice canopy adds volume and double-bounce scattering, and backscatter rises by several dB.

- Seasonal open water goes from 18.2 km² in winter to 76.3 km² in spring (sowing floods).

- The natural marshes show little open water in 2019-2020. My hypothesis is low rainfall plus groundwater pumping; rainfall and water-level data are needed to confirm it.

Why NISAR

The data used here is C-band (5.6 cm wavelength), which mostly scatters on top of the canopy. NISAR's L-band (24 cm) goes through it and can detect flooding under the vegetation, and its 12-day repeat would turn four seasonal snapshots into a real time series. The next step is to run the same processing on NISAR GCOV products over Doñana and compare both bands.

Limits

Seasonal medians hide short floods; wind roughens water and makes it brighter; a single threshold is a first approximation.

Tools

Python (NumPy, tifffile, Pillow) for processing; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the app, which runs in any browser with no server. An AI assistant (Claude) helped with code and English editing.
dataRefs: Global Seasonal Sentinel-1 Coherence and Backscatter dataset (NASA ASF DAAC)
